power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Meta-analytic structural equation modeling (MASEM) is a powerful method for research synthesis that combines the cumulative empirical work of meta-analysis with the theory-testing capabilities of structural equation modeling (Cheung & Chan, 2005; Cheung & Cheung, 2016; Jak, 2015; Jak & Cheung, 2020).
text.formatted: Meta-analytic structural equation modeling (MASEM) is a powerful method for research synthesis that combines the cumulative empirical work of meta-analysis with the theory-testing capabilities of structural equation modeling <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Cheung & Chan, 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Cheung & Cheung, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Jak, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Jak & Cheung, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: By synthesizing correlation or covariance matrices across studies, MASEM can be used to evaluate measurement models, including the dimensionality of instruments and measurement invariance across groups, as well as structural models, including mediating pathways, predictive relations, and competing theoretical accounts.

In psychometric research, MASEM has become an established tool for evaluating the factor structure, reliability, and cross-cultural generalizability of widely used instruments such as the Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale (Gnambs et al., 2018), the International Trauma Questionnaire (Kindred et al., 2026), the Positive and Negative Affect Schedule (Wedderhoff et al., 2021), and the Self-Compassion Scale (Bourke, 2026).
text.formatted: In psychometric research, MASEM has become an established tool for evaluating the factor structure, reliability, and cross-cultural generalizability of widely used instruments such as the Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Gnambs et al., 2018)</ref>, the International Trauma Questionnaire <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Kindred et al., 2026)</ref>, the Positive and Negative Affect Schedule <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Wedderhoff et al., 2021)</ref>, and the Self-Compassion Scale <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Bourke, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Other studies have used MASEM to examine the measurement precision of creativity tests (Acar et al., 2024) or attitudinal and motivational aspects of students' academic achievement (López-López et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Other studies have used MASEM to examine the measurement precision of creativity tests <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Acar et al., 2024)</ref> or attitudinal and motivational aspects of students' academic achievement <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(López-López et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: More broadly, MASEM has also been increasingly applied to synthesize substantive theory-driven models, such as technology acceptance in education (Scherer et al., 2019), models of the structure of human cognition (Emslander & Scherer, 2022), and the identification of mediating processes (Duzen et al., 2026), including mechanisms underlying intervention effects (Vints et al., 2025).
text.formatted: More broadly, MASEM has also been increasingly applied to synthesize substantive theory-driven models, such as technology acceptance in education <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Scherer et al., 2019)</ref>, models of the structure of human cognition <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Emslander & Scherer, 2022)</ref>, and the identification of mediating processes <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Duzen et al., 2026)</ref>, including mechanisms underlying intervention effects <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Vints et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: These applications demonstrate the versatility of MASEM as a research synthesis method across fields to address a broad range of research questions.
The empirical input for MASEM consists of study-level correlation or covariance matrices among the observed variables included in the measurement or structural model.

Ideally, this information is obtained from the primary data themselves, and the increasing availability of openly shared raw data has made such analyses much more feasible in recent years (e.g., Campos & Scherer, 2024; Schroeders et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Ideally, this information is obtained from the primary data themselves, and the increasing availability of openly shared raw data has made such analyses much more feasible in recent years (e.g., <ref type="bibr">Campos & Scherer, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Schroeders et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: However, data protection concerns sometimes preclude unrestricted data sharing.
In these cases, researchers must rely on summary statistics reported in primary studies.

These summary statistics can provide direct information, such as correlations or covariances reported in text, tables, or supplements, or indirect information, such as factor loadings and factor correlations from which the implied correlation matrix can be reconstructed under specific model assumptions.
Direct information is preferable because it corresponds most closely to the empirical input required for MASEM.
Yet complete correlation matrices are often omitted from the main text because of space constraints and are not consistently provided in online supplements.
This is particularly problematic for psychometric applications, where item-level matrices may involve 20 or more variables per instrument (e.g., Schroeders et al., 2024; Wedderhoff et al., 2021).
text.formatted: This is particularly problematic for psychometric applications, where item-level matrices may involve 20 or more variables per instrument (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Schroeders et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Wedderhoff et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Consequently, researchers often turn to indirect sources, most notably factor-loading matrices and factor correlations.

These quantities are more commonly reported than complete item-level correlation matrices and can approximate the original matrix when the underlying factor model fits adequately (Gnambs & Staufenbiel, 2016).
text.formatted: These quantities are more commonly reported than complete item-level correlation matrices and can approximate the original matrix when the underlying factor model fits adequately <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Gnambs & Staufenbiel, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, aggregate-data MASEM often requires extracting either directly reported statistics or model-based quantities used for matrix reconstruction.
This extraction process is labor-intensive, error-prone, and complicated by the lack of standardized reporting formats.

Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs) have created new opportunities for extracting structured information from weakly standardized scientific texts (e.g., PDF articles).

In meta-analytic research in the social and behavioral sciences, automated extraction was used early on, for example, to retrieve p-values, sample sizes, and hypothesis counts from full-text articles (Nuijten et al., 2016; Teja Lanka et al., 2021).
text.formatted: In meta-analytic research in the social and behavioral sciences, automated extraction was used early on, for example, to retrieve p-values, sample sizes, and hypothesis counts from full-text articles <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Nuijten et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Teja Lanka et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Recent work in evidence synthesis has focused on LLM-assisted data extraction for systematic reviews and meta-analyses (see Fütterer et al., 2026, for a review).

text.text: For example, Gartlehner et al. (2024) demonstrated that data elements from randomized controlled trials can be extracted with high accuracy relative to humans, while Konet et al. (2024) showed that performance depends not only on the model, but also on PDF parsing and the quality of the text made available to the model.

(2024)</ref> showed that performance depends not only on the model, but also on PDF parsing and the quality of the text made available to the model.

text.text: Broader evaluations of GPT-4 for systematic-review tasks similarly indicate that LLMs can support screening and data extraction across publication types and languages, but that performance remains task-dependent (Khraisha et al., 2024).

text.text: Recent benchmarks provide a nuanced picture by comparing LLM performance with human extraction or expert-adjudicated gold standards.

In a second-order meta-analysis context, Jansen et al. (2026) compared three LLMs with two human experts for extracting effect sizes, study counts, and participant counts from educational meta-analyses.
text.formatted: In a second-order meta-analysis context, <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Jansen et al. (2026)</ref> compared three LLMs with two human experts for extracting effect sizes, study counts, and participant counts from educational meta-analyses.

text.text: Against an expertadjudicated benchmark, the LLMs reached intraclass correlations comparable to those of the human experts, although their exact agreement was somewhat lower.

Similarly, Li et al. (2026) evaluated several LLMs for extracting statistical results, risk-of-bias assessments, and studylevel characteristics from randomized controlled trials and found high precision but consistently lower recall because models omitted relevant information.

(2026)</ref> evaluated several LLMs for extracting statistical results, risk-of-bias assessments, and studylevel characteristics from randomized controlled trials and found high precision but consistently lower recall because models omitted relevant information.

text.text: Customized prompts helped improve recall, but did not eliminate this limitation completely. Kataoka et al. (2026) also reported useful but imperfect performance for automated extraction systems based on GPT-4o and o3, with stronger performance for detecting relevant variables than for accurately extracting all numeric information.

(2026)</ref> also reported useful but imperfect performance for automated extraction systems based on GPT-4o and o3, with stronger performance for detecting relevant variables than for accurately extracting all numeric information.

text.text: These findings suggest that LLMs can be competitive with human raters for welldefined, extractive tasks, but that their performance is uneven across information types and that omissions remain a recurrent risk.
Taken together, these findings indicate that LLM-based extraction is not yet a fully autonomous process, but depends on human oversight and verification (Khraisha et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Taken together, these findings indicate that LLM-based extraction is not yet a fully autonomous process, but depends on human oversight and verification <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Khraisha et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Extraction quality depends not only on the model, but also on how the source document is represented.
Text-based pipelines are efficient when machine-readable PDFs can be reliably parsed into clean text, tables, and metadata, thereby supporting chunking, retrieval, and source linking.
Vision-based processing can be useful when relevant information depends on layout, scanned pages, complex tables, figures, or visually encoded content.

Recent surveys of document parsing describe a broader shift from modular pipelines based on optical character recognition (OCR), layout detection, and rules toward more unified systems based on large VLMs, especially for visually rich or structurally complex documents (Ke et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Recent surveys of document parsing describe a broader shift from modular pipelines based on optical character recognition (OCR), layout detection, and rules toward more unified systems based on large VLMs, especially for visually rich or structurally complex documents <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Ke et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Zhang et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: For MASEM, this matters because the required information is often distributed across tables, text, table columns, and notes, including correlation matrices, factor loadings, factor correlations, and descriptive study information.
Accordingly, the aim of this Software Focus is to introduce MASEMiner and evaluate its extraction and verification workflow for information required in MASEM.

Recent evaluations of LLMs and VLMs for evidence synthesis suggest that these systems are best understood not as replacements for expert coding, but as components of a transparent, human-in-the-loop workflow that combines automated extraction with human oversight, verification, and transparent reporting (Gartlehner et al., 2024; Khraisha et al., 2024; Konet et al., 2024; Li et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Recent evaluations of LLMs and VLMs for evidence synthesis suggest that these systems are best understood not as replacements for expert coding, but as components of a transparent, human-in-the-loop workflow that combines automated extraction with human oversight, verification, and transparent reporting <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Gartlehner et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Khraisha et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Konet et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Li et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Because LLM performance depends strongly on task specification and prompt configuration, specialized workflows are necessary for reliable AI-assisted evidence synthesis rather than generic one-size-fits-all solutions (Adam et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Because LLM performance depends strongly on task specification and prompt configuration, specialized workflows are necessary for reliable AI-assisted evidence synthesis rather than generic one-size-fits-all solutions <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Adam et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: MASEMiner provides such a workflow that is specifically designed for extracting information relevant to MASEM.
It integrates AI-assisted extraction with subsequent human verification based on the original sources.
The software is open-source and can be run locally or accessed through a hosted web application.
The source code, installation instructions, and technical documentation are available on GitHub (https://github.com/johanna-einsiedler/maseminer).
text.formatted: The source code, installation instructions, and technical documentation are available on GitHub (<ref type="url" target="https://github.com/johanna-einsiedler/maseminer">https://github.com/johanna-einsiedler/maseminer</ref>).

text.text: A hosted browser-based version is available at https://paper.metalens.tech/maseminer, which also includes a short introductory video.
text.formatted: A hosted browser-based version is available at <ref type="url" target="https://paper.metalens.tech/maseminer">https://paper.metalens.tech/maseminer</ref>, which also includes a short introductory video.

text.text: The MASEMiner extraction and verification workflow consists of four consecutive steps: (1) model configuration, (2) prompt specification, (3) document upload and extraction, and (4) human verification (see Figure 1).
text.formatted: The MASEMiner extraction and verification workflow consists of four consecutive steps: (1) model configuration, (2) prompt specification, (3) document upload and extraction, and (4) human verification (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: The Four Steps of the MASEMiner Workflow Note.
Schematic views of the interface for the direct-information task of the video gaming use case.
Step 4 shows the extraction results for Grydeland et al.
In the first step, users configure the AI model used for extraction.
Specifically, they select a provider (e.g., OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, or DeepSeek), choose a specific model version (e.g., GPT-5.6 Luna/Terra/Sol), and enter the corresponding API key.
Alternatively, users can connect any model behind an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, including locally hosted or selfhosted models served with a public address through vLLM, Ollama, or LM Studio.

For these custom models, users provide the server URL, the model name or Hugging Face model ID, and an API key placeholder if required by the interface; additional setup details are provided in the online help.
For optimal extraction performance, we recommend using the most capable currently available model from the selected provider.
Data privacy depends on where MASEMiner runs and where the model is hosted.
In the hosted version, the API key is transmitted only to the selected provider and is not stored in any database 1 .

Running MASEMiner locally avoids submitting an API key to an external web server entirely, but the content of the documents is still transmitted to the selected external model provider when a cloud API is used.

For workflows that must keep documents within a local computing environment, users can combine a local MASEMiner installation with a self-hosted model with an OpenAI-compatible endpoint as described above.

In either case, users should consult the data-retention and privacy policies of their model provider and make sure that uploading copyrighted, confidential, or unpublished material is permitted under their institutional requirements.
1 The API key passes through the server only to run the extraction and is retained in the server memory and job queue for at most 30 minutes.

The interface states this explicitly where the API key is entered ("Your API key is not stored: it passes through our server only to run the extraction (in memory and the job queue for at most 30 minutes) and is then discarded.").
In the second step, users specify the extraction task by providing the task-specific information (e.g., target variables).

MASEMiner then incorporates this information into a predefined prompt template (see Figure 1, blue-highlighted passages), alongside general extraction logic, the output schema, and review-related instructions.
text.formatted: MASEMiner then incorporates this information into a predefined prompt template (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>, blue-highlighted passages), alongside general extraction logic, the output schema, and review-related instructions.

text.text: MASEMiner supports two task types, each implemented through a parameterized prompt template tailored to MASEMspecific data structures.
The direct-information task is designed to extract correlations and related effect sizes (e.g., odds ratios) that are reported directly, either in the text or in tables.
MASEMiner extracts reported statistics in their source metric.
Any effect-size transformation or harmonization required for the subsequent synthesis is performed downstream and remains part of the analyst's meta-analytic workflow.
For this task type, users provide canonical variable labels that define the target variables in the correlation matrix that will be subjected to MASEM.
The template uses these labels to map construct-equivalent terms in the article to common matrix cells.

In addition to correlations, MASEMiner extracts scale reliabilities and sample characteristics, such as sample size, percentage of female respondents, and mean age, with links to the corresponding source evidence.
The indirect-information task is used to extract factor loadings and factor correlations from factor-analytic results to later reconstruct study-specific correlation matrices.
For this task type, users provide the measure's name and abbreviation, the number of items, and the item wording or item labels.
The template specifies how items, factors, samples, and factor-analytic solutions are represented in structured loading and factor-correlation matrices.

It also includes decision rules for handling multiple samples or competing factor solutions, preserving item order, distinguishing latent factor correlations from observed subscale correlations, and marking unavailable or ambiguous values.

In addition to the psychometric information, MASEMiner extracts sample characteristics (e.g., sample size, percentage of female respondents, and mean age), as well as analytic information (e.g., type of factor analysis and number of retained factors).
The user-supplied information is then inserted into the corresponding prompt template (Figure 1, Step 2).
text.formatted: The user-supplied information is then inserted into the corresponding prompt template (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>, <ref type="figure">Step 2</ref>).

text.text: Beyond formatting this input, the template adds four components that support extraction accuracy and the human-in-the-loop review workflow.

First, the template lists output requirements that define extraction rules identified during pilot testing to improve accuracy (e.g., unreported values must not be imputed, and numeric values must be reported as pre-computed scalars rather than arithmetic expressions).
Second, the template specifies a fixed JSON response schema, which the interactive viewer parses to populate the review interface.

Third, it includes instructions for providing an AI-assessed confidence rating for each extraction target (e.g., factor loadings, factor correlations, sample metadata), reported on a three-level ordinal scale (low, medium, high).

Fourth, it instructs the model to return an evidence snippet for each extracted value, which is displayed by the review interface alongside the corresponding value to enable rapid manual verification.

In addition to these guided prompt configurations, users can review the generated prompt (Figure 1, Step 2B) and edit the raw prompt to implement study-specific extraction rules (e.g., prioritize certain factor solutions or adapt the output schema).
text.formatted: In addition to these guided prompt configurations, users can review the generated prompt (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>, <ref type="figure">Step 2B</ref>) and edit the raw prompt to implement study-specific extraction rules (e.g., prioritize certain factor solutions or adapt the output schema).

text.text: In the third step, users upload one or more PDF files for extraction.
Before extraction begins, MASEMiner identifies whether each uploaded PDF contains a usable text layer or is a scanned document.
If the PDF contains a usable text layer, users can choose between text-based and vision-based extraction.

In text-extraction mode, the PDF text layer is parsed as Markdown (using PyMuPDF, 2026) and then sent to an LLM, which is usually faster and less expensive but depends on the quality and completeness of the native PDF text layer.

In vision mode, PDF pages are rendered as images (again using PyMuPDF, 2026) and sent to the selected multimodal model; this mode is slower and more expensive but can process scanned PDFs and visually structured tables.

In both modes, the model receives the prompt together with the document content, with each page explicitly labeled by its sequential PDF position so that evidence citations resolve back to the correct page.
If there is no text layer, extraction requires a visioncapable model.
Conversely, if the selected model does not support multimodal input, extraction is only possible when the PDF can be converted via its text layer.
After extraction, MASEMiner presents the structured results alongside the source document for human verification.

text.text: The evidence layer is generated as part of the model output.
For each extracted value, the prompt requires an evidence snippet consisting of a short quotation from the PDF, the page number, and a coarse source location (e.g., "Table 2").
text.formatted: For each extracted value, the prompt requires an evidence snippet consisting of a short quotation from the PDF, the page number, and a coarse source location (e.g., "Table <ref type="table">2"</ref>).

text.text: Each evidence snippet is tagged with a JSON-path identifier that links the quotation to the corresponding extracted field.

To produce a highlight, MASEMiner searches the PDF's native text layer for the snippet. 2 The resulting text locations are returned to the browser, which displays them as semi-transparent highlights over the rendered PDF page.

text.text: Because this step requires a machine-readable text layer, highlighting depends on the PDF being natively typeset, independently of whether the extraction itself ran in text or vision mode.
For scanned image-only pages, the page reference is still shown, but the passage cannot be highlighted.

When researchers click an extracted value, the viewer scrolls to the evidence page and emphasizes the corresponding highlight, allowing the value to be checked against the original source in a single action.
Edits of the extracted values are tracked as human corrections.
Results can be exported in JSON format, preserving the original model output, prompt, model information, evidence links, and manual overrides.
In this way, MASEMiner supports not only efficient extraction but also transparency, verification, and an audit trail for subsequent meta-analytic work.
In addition, the structured results can be exported as a CSV file, facilitating further analysis with statistical software.
To evaluate the extraction accuracy of MASEMiner, we used four meta-analytic databases from previous research that provided human-coded reference data.
These databases were selected to cover two task types central to MASEM.
First, we considered direct information, that is, statistical information explicitly reported in text, tables, or matrices, such as zero-order correlations and related effect sizes.

Second, we considered indirect information, that is, information that must be reconstructed from psychometric analyses reported in primary studies, such as factor loading patterns, factor correlations, and factor-analytic metadata.
All extractions were conducted with the most recent OpenAI model available at the time of evaluation (GPT-5.6 Sol, accessed September 2026).
The prompts used for the extractions, the exact JSON output, the reference databases, and the evaluation scripts are available in the online repository.
The four use cases were selected because each provided a suitable benchmark based on detailed, human-coded extraction protocols.
For each information type, we drew on two published meta-analytic databases and sampled a subset of primary studies (k = 10).
For each information type, the studies sampled from one database were used during prompt development, whereas the studies sampled from the second database were kept separate and used as a held-out
Our extraction tasks differed from standard binary classification, since the number of potentially extractable values was not fixed in advance for several of the targets.
For example, a correlation-matrix cell for a given sample may contain more than one eligible effect size (e.g., measured with different instruments).
Similarly, the number of factor loadings and factor correlations depends on the number of factors identified in a given sample.
We therefore evaluated performance using metrics that do not require a predefined set of true negatives (e.g., specificity or conventional cell-level accuracy).

Instead, we evaluated extraction performance against a reference database for each use case: the values coded in the original meta-analysis were double-checked against the primary publications for the present study.
Each comparison yields four counts (Table 1).
text.formatted: Each comparison yields four counts (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>).

text.text: A true positive (TP) is a reference value that was correctly recovered by the LLM.

Three conceptually distinct types of errors were differentiated: (1) omissions (OMIT), where the LLM fails to report a value contained in the reference database; (2) overextractions (OVER), where the LLM reports a value for which no reference value exists (e.g., a correlation for a variable pair or a sample that was not a target of the meta-analysis); and (3) wrong values (WRONG), where the LLM reports a value that does not match the reference value.

We did not distinguish between wrong-sample and wrong-variable assignments as separate categories, since they are already contained in these counts (e.g., a loading assigned to a wrong factor is counted as two wrong values).
Empirically, such misassignments were practically non-existent (6 of 2,397 target values, or 0.25%, all due to three items of one publication that were assigned to a neighboring factor).

These counts map onto false negatives (FN) and false positives (FP) as follows: an omission is a false negative, an overextraction is a false positive, and a wrong value is counted as both-a false positive, because it is an erroneous output, and a false negative, because the true value was not recovered (FN = OMIT + WRONG, FP = OVER + WRONG).
A wrong value is therefore penalized twice.

We adopted this conservative scoring deliberately, since omissions and overextractions are relatively easy for a human reviewer to spot, whereas wrong values are not immediately obvious and thus an error is more likely to pass unnoticed into the synthesis.

Based on these counts, we computed sensitivity (recall), precision, and Jaccard overlap (Tharwat, 2021); Tables 2 and 3 report these metrics together with the absolute numbers of omissions, overextractions, and wrong values, so that readers can judge the verification burden behind each index.

text.text: Because multiple extracted values are nested within the same publication and are therefore not independent, the pooled indices should not be interpreted as independent tests of the extraction system.

We therefore additionally computed SEN, PRE, and JAC separately for each primary publication; these publication-level results are reported in the online supplement (Tables S1-S4) to show between-document variability in extraction performance.

text.text: The first direct-information use case was based on Gnambs (2013), which served as a prompt-development case.
text.formatted: The first direct-information use case was based on <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Gnambs (2013)</ref>, which served as a prompt-development case.

text.text: The original meta-analysis examined correlations among self-and other ratings of the Big Five personality traits from a multitrait-multi-informant perspective.

For this purpose, the study reconstructed a 10 × 10 correlation matrix comprising the five Big Five traits assessed by self-ratings and peer ratings and conducted separate meta-analyses for the unique correlations in this matrix.

This use case was well suited for developing the directinformation extraction prompt because the relevant information consisted of explicitly reported zero-order correlations, but these values had to be selected from a complex literature base in which studies could report multiple samples, multiple instruments, subgroup results, reliabilities, and overlapping correlations.

A random sample of 10 primary studies included in the metaanalysis was therefore used to refine the prompt rules for identifying eligible correlations, distinguishing target from non-target effects, and extracting associated study and sample information.

To evaluate the complete human-in-the-loop workflow, four coders (student research assistants trained in meta-analytic coding) verified the MASEMiner output in the interface and, where necessary, corrected, deleted, or added values.

For the MASEMiner workflow, the time for uploading the documents and running the automated extraction was recorded once per use case and added to the individual verification time.

MASEMiner is part of a broader movement toward using AI in research synthesis (Fütterer et al., 2026).
text.formatted: MASEMiner is part of a broader movement toward using AI in research synthesis <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Fütterer et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: It was designed to support researchers in extracting information required for meta-analytic structural equation modeling, including zero-order correlations reported in tables and text, as well as indirect information that can be used to reconstruct correlation matrices, such as factor loadings and factor correlations.

Across four use cases, the system achieved high extraction accuracy, and the verification study showed that automated extraction followed by human verification reduced coding time by 42% relative to conventional manual extraction at comparable accuracy.
An open question is whether the extraction accuracy of MASEMiner can be improved further.

It should be noted that the current performance is already on a par with that of trained human coders and that a considerable part of the remaining discrepancies stems from contradictory or ambiguous information in the primary studies.
Nevertheless, further improvements are conceivable.
First, several agents could code the same source independently, with the final values determined by consensus scoring (e.g., majority voting across runs).

Second, additional plausibility checks could be implemented, together with explicit disambiguation rules for cases in which a source offers several admissible values (e.g., multiple samples or factor solutions).

Moreover, the use of AI in research synthesis is not restricted to extracting statistical information from published articles, but may also support literature search and study screening (König et al., 2024 (König et al., , 2026)).
text.formatted: Moreover, the use of AI in research synthesis is not restricted to extracting statistical information from published articles, but may also support literature search and study screening <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(König et al., 2024</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(König et al., , 2026))</ref>.

text.text: It is also possible to integrate downstream analytical functionality, such as pooling reconstructed correlation matrices, transforming extracted statistics into a common effect size metric, or generating draft reports.

Tools such as MASEMiner could be extended toward more automated forms of evidence collection and preparation, analogous to large-scale synthesis platforms such as Neurosynth (Yarkoni et al., 2011) and the more recent Neurosynth Compose (Kent et al., 2026), which combine automated data extraction, centralized databases, and expert-guided curation to make cumulative evidence more accessible and reusable.

text.text: At this stage, however, we intentionally refrain from implementing such end-to-end automation.

Instead, MASEMiner focuses on extraction and human verification while keeping analysis as a separate step to preserve transparency and ensure that automation supports rather than replaces expert judgment.
Accordingly, the present evaluation targets the accuracy and efficiency of the extraction and verification workflow rather than the downstream MASEM results.
Such results depend on additional application-specific decisions, including effect-size transformations, matrix reconstruction, pooling, and model specification.

More generally, the increasing use of AI in research synthesis underscores the importance of reproducibility in AI-assisted research, an issue that has received insufficient attention to date. Schroeders et al. (2026) argue that the level of reproducibility in AI-assisted research should be distinguished according to its role in the research process.

text.text: When AI is used as a research partner to support brainstorming, editing, or drafting, transparent disclosure may often be sufficient.
By contrast, when AI is used as a methodological instrument, its outputs enter the evidential chain and therefore require more detailed documentation.
MASEMiner falls into the latter category because the extracted values provide the empirical basis for subsequent meta-analytic analyses.
For this reason, we provide not only the extracted values but also the corresponding human revisions in JSON format.
This makes the audit process transparent, allows users to trace how AI-generated outputs were reviewed and modified, and supports the reproducibility of the extraction workflow.
Several limitations need to be considered.

First, the default prompts were designed to be as generic as possible, avoiding idiosyncratic features of the validation databases that could lead to prompt overfitting and reduce generalizability to other applications.
Our initial validation indicated that extraction performance remains high.

Nevertheless, because prompt design is known to substantially affect LLM performance, it is impossible to cover all potential applications with a single universal prompt or a one-size-fits-all approach (Adam et al., 2026; Sahoo et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Nevertheless, because prompt design is known to substantially affect LLM performance, it is impossible to cover all potential applications with a single universal prompt or a one-size-fits-all approach <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Adam et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Sahoo et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Some degree of prompt adaptation will therefore likely be necessary when applying MASEMiner to new research domains, instruments, or extraction targets (e.g., higherorder factor models).

The structured prompt and output schema can in principle be extended to additional summary statistics, such as means and standard deviations, or study characteristics, such as respondents' mean educational level or assessment modes, when these are required for a specific synthesis.
However, these targets were not evaluated in the present study, and the extraction accuracy of other information remains to be established.

Moreover, very long full-text documents were excluded from the TAS-20 prompt-development set, so that the reported accuracy does not cover unusually long documents, dissertations, or reports with extensive supplementary material, for which context limits may pose additional challenges.

Second, given the very high extraction accuracy for most targets, users may be prone to automation bias, placing excessive trust in the AI-generated output and conducting less thorough human verification than is required for a genuinely human-in-the-loop extraction workflow (e.g., Klingbeil et al., 2024).

text.text: Our verification study is consistent with this concern: coders rarely deleted surplus effect sizes, and wrong values that required consulting the source table were corrected only in part.
Finally, the extraction performance reported here is based on the most recent OpenAI model available at the time of validation.

We deliberately refrained from benchmarking individual LLMs because our focus was on the tool and its workflow rather than on model comparisons, and because LLM performance may change rapidly with model updates (Chen et al., 2024).

text.text: MASEMiner provides a workflow for AI-assisted extraction of heterogeneous statistical information required for MASEM, including directly reported correlations and indirect information needed to reconstruct correlation matrices.

Across four use cases, factor loadings were recovered almost perfectly, and directly reported effect sizes were recovered completely, although with surplus candidates that users can delete in the interface.
In combination with human verification, the workflow reduced coding time by 42% relative to conventional manual extraction at comparable accuracy.
Editable outputs, links to the source evidence, and a JSON export that preserves both the original model output and all human corrections keep the extraction process transparent and verifiable.

The prompt-development cases were used to refine the generic extraction prompt, clarify variable definitions, and resolve recurring ambiguities in the extraction rules.

The independent evaluation cases were not used during prompt development, rather they served to examine whether the resulting generic prompt generalized to new extraction tasks within the same broad information type.
For direct information, the prompt-development case was based on Gnambs (2013), which required extracting correlations among self-and other ratings of the Big Five personality traits.
The independent evaluation case was based on Marker et al. (2022), which required extracting effect sizes and study information on sedentary video gaming and body mass.

For indirect information, the prompt-development case was based on a database that was used to examine the dimensionality of a clinical measure, the Toronto Alexithymia Scale (TAS-20; Schroeders et al., 2022), which required extracting factor loadings, factor correlations, and factor-analytic information.

The independent evaluation case was based on the Need for Cognition Scale (NCS-18; Schroeders et al., 2024), which tested whether the same generic extraction logic transferred to a different scale and a different MASEM context.
